title: Baron
contribution: Version read: v4.0 (BARON User's Manual, revision of 28 June 2000, sole author line). It states branch-and-reduce (duality- and probing-based optimality range reduction, poor man's LPs, McCormick factorable relaxations, finiteness-oriented branching) on two traced examples, and documents BARON's 1991-2000 growth, its eleven specialized modules beside the factorable NLP module, its options with defaults and its user exits.
problem_entry: Nonconvex problems with several local optima across engineering and the sciences; BARON named for combining interval analysis and duality in a reduce arsenal with branch and bound; each version tied to the applications it was first used on (v4.0, pp. 7-8).
key_idea: Branch-and-reduce: reduction tests at every node in pre- and post-processing, node solved again when reduction is significant; optimality-based reduction from duals and the incumbent (x_j >= x_j^U - (U - L)/lambda_j), probing, poor man's LPs at nodes with the 2n bound LPs solved once at the root; McCormick relaxations; violation branching with periodic bisection and incumbent branching (v4.0, pp. 15-24).
assumptions: Finite variable bounds as inputs of the core (p. 56); duality-based tests need a convex relaxation solved with duals (p. 20); factorable module limited to exp, ln, x^alpha, beta^x (p. 41); optimality-based inequalities may cut feasible points but none better than U (p. 16).
proof_devices: value-function argument: a Lagrange multiplier gives a supporting hyperplane of the perturbation function, whose intersection with the level U bounds the variable (pp. 12, 15)
reduction rules tabulated by active constraint / requirement / valid inequality, probing rows included (Tables 2.1-2.2, pp. 16-17)
constructed pathological case for poor man's LPs (Fig. 2.5.f) and why it cannot arise after the root LPs (p. 19)
finiteness through periodic bisection (exhaustiveness) and branching at the incumbent (p. 24)
experiments: No benchmark; two traced examples. Example 1: separable relaxation 5 nodes, factorable relaxation solves it at the root, marginals plus probing prove optimality without branching, incumbent branching 3 nodes instead of 5 (pp. 25-31). Example 2 (concave QP): bisection branch and bound 17 iterations, branch-and-reduce 7 (p. 32).
positioning: Builds on McCormick's factorable programming (pp. 20, 104); the bibliography is mostly his group's application papers (pp. 103-105); students and NYU collaborators credited for modules (pp. 8-9).
writing: Didactic manual: the algorithm in figures plus two toy instances traced node by node with bounds (pp. 12-35); a history paragraph with code size per version (pp. 7-8); every option tabulated with its default (pp. 46-53).
limits_future: Compiled library free for non-commercial use (pp. 8, 44-45); FP only under OSL, few NLP and SDP interfaces, more interfaces left to future plans (p. 43); the general module does not exploit the special classes' structure (p. 41); v4.0 defaults: probing off, absolute tolerance 1e-6, relative 0 (pp. 46, 49).

method_links.note: Version v4.0. Reductions at every node in pre- and post-processing, relaxation rebuilt while reduction is significant (maxredpass, maxnodepass); cheap poor man's LPs at nodes, exact bound LPs once at the root; probing off by default and only feasibility-based tightening in preprocessing; reductions scale with U - L.

Version v4.0. One code base grown from 1800 GAMS lines (1991-93) to about 26,000 F90 plus 17,000 C lines (v4.0), each version applied to new classes, students credited; every reduction family switchable; per-component CPU-time file on by default.
Version v4.0. The factorable NLP module allows an entirely LP-based approach and uses a linear relaxation by default.
Version v4.0. The IQP module defaults to a quadratic relaxation (qplin 0) and may call the QP solvers of OSL, MINOS or SNOPT: in 2000 the LP default did not hold for quadratic programs.

Version v4.0. Eleven specialized class modules (separable concave, fixed charge, fractional, multiplicative, indefinite QP, MILP, mixed-integer SDP and others) beside the general factorable module; specialized concave codes already in 1994-95.

transferable: Tabulate bound-tightening rules as active constraint / requirement / valid inequality, so that each rule's precondition is explicit (Tables 2.1-2.2, pp. 16-17).
When a cheap heuristic replaces an exact subproblem, construct the case where it fails completely and state where in the algorithm that case is excluded (p. 19).
Teach the algorithm inside the manual on a two-variable instance, rerunning it under each device (relaxation type, reduction on or off, branching rule) and counting nodes (pp. 25-31).

Expose every search component as a user exit with a fixed signature (range reduction, lower bounding, feasibility test, random start, branching, local search, objective) so that a new class reuses the core (pp. 55-61).
Write a per-component CPU-time breakdown on every run, so that the cost of each device can be read from ordinary runs (p. 51; logs pp. 65-66, 94).
coauthors: None on the v4.0 title page (sole author line N. V. Sahinidis); 17 students credited, Tawarmalani singled out; Overton and Wilkins (NYU) for the mixed-integer SDP module (pp. 1, 8-9). The Scholar entry for the 2005 edition lists N Sahinidis, M Tawarmalani.

quotes.text: As the emphasis is on range reduction, we refer to the resulting algorithm as a branch and reduce algorithm.
A linear relaxation is used by default.

title: Gams
contribution: The GAMS/BARON solver manual (31 March 2005, BARON 7.2.5, with Tawarmalani) sets BARON's contract with GAMS users: finite bounds on all nonlinear expressions, allowed functions, termination statuses and the actions they call for, multiple-solution and multi-start modes, and defaults for every reduction, relaxation and branching option.
problem_entry: GAMS users who need global NLP and MINLP solutions: traditional algorithms converge only under convexity, BARON's branch-and-bound under fairly general assumptions, the first being finite bounds on variables and expressions (p. 1).
key_idea: Branch-and-bound with propagation and duality-based range reduction exposed as options: four reduction families plus probing on all branching variables every third level on by default, capped reduction passes and relaxation rebuilds per node, LP relaxation with outer approximators, dynamic branching, several solutions from one tree, relaxation-only and convex constraint classes (pp. 2, 5-6, 9-12).
assumptions: All nonlinear variables and expressions finitely bounded (finite variable bounds do not imply finite expression bounds, 1/x on [0, 1]); otherwise globality is not guaranteed and BARON may stop; functions exp, ln, x^alpha, beta^x, x^y, |x|, no trigonometric functions (p. 2); bounds also as solver or expression bounds in the option file (pp. 7-8).
experiments: none; one annotated log (gear.gms) with time split into parsing, preprocessing, navigating, relaxed, local, tightening, marginals and probing (pp. 3-4).
positioning: Contrasts BARON with NLP and MINLP algorithms that converge only under convexity (p. 1); multiple solutions without integer cuts (p. 5); points to the Tawarmalani-Sahinidis 2002 book for details (p. 5).
writing: Reference manual ordered contract first (licenses, bounds, functions), then the log and termination messages with user actions, features, and option tables with defaults (pp. 1-13).
limits_future: Needs a GAMS/BARON license and a licensed LP solver; no trigonometric functions (p. 2); defaults epsa 1e-9 and epsr 0.1 (= GAMS optcr), so Normal Completion allows U - L up to 0.1|L| (pp. 4, 8; my reading of the definitions); no future work stated.

method_links.note: Range reduction is the default node operation, with reduction passes and relaxation rebuilds capped (maxredpass 10, maxnodepass 5) and probing scheduled by depth (pstart, pend, pfreq 3). Against v4.0 (S097 p. 49), probing moved from off to on by default. The guarantee rests on finite expression bounds (the Method 1 limitation).
Every reduction family can be switched off (tdo, mdo, lbttdo, obttdo, pdo = 0) and the log splits time by component: the switches and the instrumentation an ablation needs.
LP relaxation by default (nlpdolin 1); convex functions enter as outer-approximating cuts with set counts and rounds; constraints declared convex become supporting-hyperplane cuts.
Physically meaningful bounds on all variables named the best way to give bounds; relaxation-only constraints (for instance first-order optimality conditions) passed apart from the model.
Numerical difficulties are to be reported to the developers.

Missing bounds void the global guarantee and are reported as such (Search Terminated by BARON); the multi-start mode is titled a heuristic solver, for insight into local solutions. The explicit sentence SKILL.md quotes for Heuristic 7 is not in this edition.

transferable: In a solver's documentation, list each termination status with what it means for the guarantee and what the user should do next (pp. 4-5).
Offer a preprocessing-only mode (maxiter 0) and document which reduction switches to set to zero to sample local minima without range reduction (p. 6).
Keep a function's argument away from its singularity with an expression bound in the option file (z = x - y with z.lo 0.00001 for log(z)) instead of editing the model (pp. 7-8).
Read the default relative tolerance before calling a run global: epsr is 0.1 at these defaults (p. 8).
Compare the option tables of successive manual editions to date when a component became a default (probing: off in S097 v4.0 p. 49, every third level here, pp. 9-10).

quotes.text: If this step fails, global optimality of the solutions provided is not guaranteed.
Maximum number of times range reduction is performed at a node before a new relaxation is constructed.

title: Polynomial-time algorithms for the integer minimal principle for centrosymmetric structures
contribution: Reduces the integer minimal principle for centrosymmetric phasing to a homogeneous linear system over F2 and solves it globally by O(M^2 T) binary Gauss-Jordan or sparse Markowitz elimination: identical optima and 34-45 times faster than CPLEX branch-and-bound on 18 structures, better R values than SHELXS on all 38.
problem_entry: The IP formulation of Vaia and Sahinidis 2003 is exact, but branch-and-bound may need exponentially many iterations, while its LP gap is observed to be zero; entry through solution properties seen in many computations (pp. 2-3).
key_idea: With tau_t fixed at 0 (where the relaxation can be expected to have its minimum), the IP becomes a homogeneous system mod 2 whose nonzero null-space vectors are global solutions; solved by binary Gauss-Jordan (row additions only) or sparse Markowitz elimination; the IP is needed only if no nontrivial solution exists (pp. 3-5).
assumptions: Centrosymmetric structures, so phases 0 or pi and triplet cosines -1 or 1 (p. 2); N:M:T = 1:10:100 with the strongest reflections (p. 3); a nonzero solution of M3 exists, argued from Sayre's equation and found on all 38 structures (pp. 5-6).
proof_devices: equivalence chain M1 -> M2 -> M3 from the IP to a linear system over F2 (pp. 3-4)
division- and multiplication-free Gauss-Jordan elimination over F2, O(M^2 T) (p. 4)
sparse column-major Gaussian elimination with the Markowitz pivot rule, same complexity, much less memory (pp. 4-5)
Sayre's equation as the reason a nontrivial solution exists for strong reflections (p. 5)
complexity O(N^3) at the standard ratio and O(N^6) if M grows like N^2 (p. 8)
experiments: 18 structures against CPLEX 7.0 (identical global minima, PA1 and PA2 34 and 45 times faster on average, Table 2, p. 6); 20 more structures all solved (Table 4, p. 7); resolution truncated from 0.9 to 1.3 Å (Table 5, pp. 7-8); 38 structures against SHELXS at defaults, better R on all (Table 6, pp. 7-8); one 1.5 GHz Xeon (p. 5).
positioning: Continues Vaia and Sahinidis 2003 and the minimal principle of Debaerdemaeker and Woolfson (p. 2); contrasts deterministic global optimization with the stochastic SHELX codes, which do not exploit the phase problem's structure (p. 7).
writing: The abstract states the move (observed solution properties -> linear system over F2) and the results; comparison tables with averages and standard deviations; the interpretation of the comparison is a separate paragraph (pp. 2, 6-8).
limits_future: The minimal principle with CRUNCH peak picking fails below about 1.2-1.3 Å; SHELXS ran at defaults and could be tuned; SHELXD solves all structures but at least ten times slower (p. 7); centrosymmetric structures only; no future-work section.

method_links.note: The cheap structural inference is pushed to the end: the reduction removes enumeration altogether (no branch-and-bound), with the IP kept as fallback when the reduced system has only the trivial solution.
The fast method is checked against an exact solver's global minima on the same 18 structures; the domain baseline's developer is consulted and his assessment reported.
SHELXS runs at its defaults rather than in its strongest mode; the authors say so and show one tuned rerun.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Empirical regularity turned into an exact reduction
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Zero LP gaps and a relaxation minimum expected at tau = 0, seen across computations, are used to fix tau and reduce the IP to a linear system over F2; the IP stays as fallback.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Global optimum as a test of the scientific model
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: With no false minima, truncating the data resolution shows unambiguously where the minimal principle with peak picking fails (about 1.2-1.3 Å).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Linearize through discreteness of the domain
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Centrosymmetry makes phases 0 or pi and cosines -1 or 1, so the trigonometric terms are replaced by binary variables (formulation of Vaia and Sahinidis 2003).

transferable: When an IP's LP bound is tight on every instance you run, look at which variables sit at a fixed value in the LP solutions, and check whether fixing them leaves an exact structured system (pp. 2-4).
Over F2, eliminate with row additions only (no multiplication or division); when rows have at most three nonzeros, switch to a sparse column-major structure with Markowitz pivots (pp. 4-5).
Validate a fast special-purpose method against an exact general solver on the same instances: first identical optimal values, then time and memory (p. 6).
Use a global solution to find where a scientific model breaks: degrade the data step by step and record where the certified optimum stops recovering the known answer (pp. 7-8).
Against a domain baseline run at defaults, say that tuning could help, show one tuned run, and report what the baseline's developer says (p. 7).

quotes.text: Instead, properties of the solution of the optimization problem, as observed in a large number of computational experiments, are exploited in order to reduce the optimization formulation to a system of linear equations in the number field of two elements (F2).
Since our algorithm provides the global solution to the minimal principle model and there is no false minima issue, we are able to identify unambiguously the resolution …

title: Selection, acquisition, and allocation of manufacturing technology in a multi-period environment
contribution: Version read: preprint (June 20, 2000, titled '... in a Multi-Product Environment'). Proves the multiperiod technology selection, acquisition and allocation MILP NP-hard and gives an LP-based temporal capacity shifting heuristic that is asymptotically optimal almost surely, which also explains why LP and Lagrangian gaps shrink with longer planning horizons.
problem_entry: Heuristics for capacity expansion are justified only empirically (p. 4), and relaxation gaps are observed not to grow, even to fall, with the horizon length despite NP-hardness (pp. 11-12).
key_idea: Solve the LP relaxation, keep the allocations, shift capacity additions to earlier LP acquisition periods up to availability, round up: at most one extra acquisition per technology over the LP (Lemma 4.3), so the error vanishes relative to z_IP as the horizon grows (pp. 12-21).
assumptions: No inventory or disposal, discounted costs (p. 7); constant procurement bound for exposition, lifted in the appendix (pp. 14, 24); random models D1-D3 with feasibility via an artificial technology (pp. 15-16); unit production cost and demand scaled to at least 1 (p. 19).
proof_devices: NP-hardness by instance mapping from capacitated lot sizing with zero holding costs (Lemma 3.1, Theorem 1, pp. 9-11)
counting lemma: at most one more acquisition per technology than the LP (Lemma 4.3, pp. 14-15)
extreme order statistics: the maximum of i.i.d. nonnegative variables with finite second moment is o(sqrt n) almost surely, of independent ones with bounded moments o(n) (Lemmas 5.1-5.2, pp. 16-17)
error sandwich 0 <= z_H - z_IP <= z_H - z_LP (Theorem 3, p. 18)
z_IP = Omega(n) from an explicit dual-feasible solution (Corollary 3.1, pp. 19-20)
asymptotic tightness of the LP and Lagrangian relaxations (Corollary 3.2, pp. 20-21)
experiments: Random instances of a two-family network with two dedicated, one flexible and one artificial technology, ten samples per point: convergence under D1-D3 and sensitivity to demand and cost variance, to the fixed-to-variable cost ratio, and flexible share under correlated demand (pp. 21-23; Tables 1-5, p. 28); plots not readable (pp. 29-32).
positioning: Generalizes Rajagopalan 1994, Li and Tirupati 1994 and Fong and Srinivasan 1981 (p. 8); continues Liu and Sahinidis 1997 and Ahmed and Sahinidis 1999 (p. 4); explains the observations of Chang and Gavish 1995 and Liu and Sahinidis 1995 (pp. 11-12, 20).
writing: A roadmap paragraph names each section's result (p. 5); the simplifying assumption is flagged and lifted in an appendix (pp. 14, 24); the computations are framed as secondary to the theory (p. 21).
limits_future: Guarantee asymptotic in the horizon length; heuristic in its simple form, improvable by cost-aware shifting or by combining it with other heuristics (p. 15); no inventory or disposal (p. 7); the preprint has no conclusion section.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Empirical regularity turned into a theorem
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The counter-intuitive observation that LP and Lagrangian gaps do not grow with the horizon despite NP-hardness is explained by the heuristic's asymptotic optimality and Corollary 3.2.

transferable: Prove a planning model NP-hard by mapping every instance of a known NP-hard special case (capacitated lot sizing) onto a single-technology instance, with the feasible sets equivalent in both directions (pp. 9-11).
Design an LP-rounding heuristic around one counting property (at most one more fixed charge per resource than the LP pays), because that is the property the error bound needs (pp. 14-15, 18).
For an asymptotic relative-error result, lower-bound the optimum linearly in n with a hand-built dual-feasible solution (pp. 19-20).
Make random test instances feasible by construction with an expensive artificial resource of unlimited capacity (pp. 16, 21).

quotes.text: However, the qualitative justification of these heuristics has been based upon empirical evidence.
In the next section, we provide a mathematical explanation of this phenomenon using the heuristic strategy developed next.

title: SnB version 2.3: triplet sieve phasing for centrosymmetric structures
contribution: Builds the triplet sieve (starts from an integer minimal principle) into the SnB direct-methods program as version 2.3, behind an applicability test with automatic fallback and with size-scaled default parameters, cutting the time to solution 4.1 to 98.5 times on 14 of 15 centrosymmetric test structures.
problem_entry: SnB's time to solution depends on the refinement-cycle cost and on the share of random trials that refine to solutions; better-than-random starts from the sieve raise that share (p. 2).
key_idea: A sieve subroutine generates trial phase sets for centrosymmetric structures under 100 atoms, reduces the sieve phases when degrees of freedom are too many, and reverts to standard SnB when trials are unsatisfactory; three new parameters as functions of N (pp. 3, 8).
assumptions: Centrosymmetric structures; large-|E| triplets have phase 0, so NSP must stay small enough to exclude 180-degree triplets, above a minimum NSP; fewer than about 100 atoms in the asymmetric unit; degrees of freedom vary with origin fixing (pp. 2-3).
experiments: 15 centrosymmetric data sets; parameters tuned on these test jobs and the defaults timed on the same sets; solutions identified by mean phase error against phases from the known coordinates; 4.1-98.5 times faster on 14 of 15 (average factor 29.5), one structure slower (ratio 0.47) (pp. 4-7).
positioning: Places the sieve beside SHELXD's Patterson-based starting atoms as another way to beat random starts (p. 2).
writing: Short program note: abstract, method with a flow chart, test table, defaults table, availability URL (pp. 1-8).
limits_future: Centrosymmetric structures under about 100 atoms only (pp. 2-3); released as SnB 2.3 with automatic solution detection (p. 7). Not stated by the authors: defaults tuned and evaluated on the same 15 structures, and the slower structure is not discussed (pp. 4-7).

method_links.note: The method lands as a module of a long-lived production program and ships as a named version with defaults, but the host is the SnB program distributed from hwi.buffalo.edu, not his own solver.
Success defined against known answers (mean phase error against phases from the known coordinates); per-structure ratios reported, the one slowdown included.
Defaults tuned on the same 15 structures used to report the gain; no hold-out (compare SKILL.md Inner Tension 5).
The new component enters behind an applicability test and with an automatic fallback to the old path, the design Method 5 step 4 asks of nonlinear relaxations, here in a crystallography code.

transferable: Integrate a new start procedure into an existing code behind an applicability test, with an automatic fallback to the old procedure when the new one cannot produce acceptable trials (p. 3).
Express new parameters as functions of instance size so that the defaults carry across sizes (Table 2, p. 8).
Report per-instance speed-up ratios and keep the instance that got slower in the table (Table 1, pp. 6-7).
coauthors: Hongliang Xu (first and corresponding author), Alexander B. Smith, Charles M. Weeks (p. 1)

quotes.text: If satisfactory trial structures cannot be generated, the variable ‘UseSieve’ is set to FALSE, and the program reverts to standard SnB operation using trial structures with randomly positioned atoms.
This comparison shows that the computing time required for 14 of the 15 test structures is reduced by a factor of 4.1 to 98.5 when sieving is included.

title: Sparse matrix binormalization on a GPU
contribution: A 4-page extended abstract (proceedings never published, per the CV note) proposing a CUDA implementation of the Livne-Golub binormalization (BIN) scaling algorithm on an NVIDIA G80 GPU, arguing its fit to SIMD hardware and announcing large speed-ups for a final version without measurements.
problem_entry: BIN lowers condition numbers more than other scaling methods but costs two to four times as much as simple diagonal scaling; a 2006 GPU offers about ten times a CPU's peak (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: One thread per row of BIN's main loop, because rows are independent, each row update is costly, no branch divergence occurs and the large arrays are read-only (pp. 3-4).
assumptions: A real symmetric and scalable; no a priori bound on the convergence factor, convergence for every scalable A, nearly optimal conditioning under Property A (p. 3); NVIDIA G80 architecture (p. 2).
experiments: none; three properties announced for the final version: orders of magnitude faster than the CPU code, near-peak GFLOPS, better scaling in the number of nonzeros (p. 4).
positioning: Builds on Livne and Golub's BIN and on early GPU linear-algebra codes (pp. 1-2).
writing: Background on the GPU and on BIN, then the fit argument, with results in the future tense (pp. 2-4).
limits_future: No measurements (p. 4); the text draws no link to an optimization solver (pp. 1-4); the proceedings were never published (work-list note).

method_links.note: Same logic outside relaxations: a stronger method (better conditioning) is held back by its cost, and the plan lowers the cost with hardware; nothing was measured, so it is not evidence of a bound-per-second test.

transferable: Before porting a kernel to a GPU, check three properties of its main loop: independent row work, no branch divergence within a warp, and read-only access to the large arrays (pp. 3-4).

quotes.text: In this paper, an NVIDIA GeForce G80 GPU is used to mitigate this expense.
It is therefore anticipated that the GPU implementation of this algorithm that will be reported in the final version of this paper will exhibit the following properties

title: Direct space and simultaneous direct-reciprocal space optimization models for phasing structures (abstract P02.02.06)
contribution: A poster abstract (Acta Cryst. A64, C202, identified from the file) proposing two MILP phasing models with direct-space constraints, electron density sampled on a grid with data-derived bounds and one model also in reciprocal space, to extend combinatorial phasing to non-centrosymmetric crystals.
problem_entry: The sieve method works for centrosymmetric structures; aims are a more robust model with odd triplets and, mainly, a combinatorial-optimization approach for non-centrosymmetric crystals (p. 1).
key_idea: Electron density sampled on a grid, structure factors at grid points written in the integer variables that describe the phases, bounds from experimental data; one model also in reciprocal space (p. 1).
assumptions: None stated beyond grid sampling and data-derived bounds (p. 1).
experiments: Computational results for several structures announced, without numbers (p. 1).
positioning: Follows the triplet sieve of Smith, Xu and Sahinidis 2007, its reference [1] (p. 1).
writing: One-paragraph poster abstract: aim, models, an announced computational section (p. 1).
limits_future: No results, limits or follow-up in the abstract (p. 1).

method_links.note: From the special class already solved (centrosymmetric) to the general one (non-centrosymmetric).
Problem knowledge (experimental data, direct-space physics) enters the model as bounds and constraints.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Linearize through discreteness of the domain
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Integer variables describe the phases in MILP phasing models, now extended to non-centrosymmetric crystals (compare S198 p. 2); whether the models are exact is not stated.

transferable: Strengthen a formulation with constraints from a second representation of the same object (direct-space density on a grid beside reciprocal-space phase relations), bounded by the measured data (p. 1).

quotes.text: The purpose of the current work is to develop a more robust model for accurate phasing in the presence of odd triplets, and more important, to provide a combinatorial optimization approach to phasing non-centrosymmetric crystals.
Direct space is constrained through sampling of electron density on a grid.

title: Multiterm polyhedral relaxations for nonconvex, quadratically constrained quadratic programs
contribution: Derives polyhedral multiterm relaxations of QCQP from the convex envelope of each constraint's whole bilinear part, characterizes its facets as LP basic solutions, separates them by cutting planes with UBQP-priced column generation, and shows on 135 random QCQPs that root cuts passed to BARON solve more instances (98 against 75 of 135 by Table 2) in less time.
problem_entry: Practice, BARON and LINDO included, relaxes quadratic constraints term by term because termwise relaxations stay polyhedral in the original variables; whole-constraint relaxations are tighter; the entry is to keep polyhedrality and relax the sum of bilinear terms jointly (p. 2).
key_idea: Nonvertical facets of a multilinear function's convex envelope over a box are exactly the basic feasible solutions of an LP over the box vertices (Theorem 2.4); add them on demand by Algorithm MUL (most violated facet for the function with the largest underestimation gap), solving the separation LP by column generation priced by an unconstrained binary QP (pp. 5, 7-15).
assumptions: Variables in a nonempty bounded box (p. 1); polyhedral envelope, true on boxes, with a counterexample on other domains (p. 3); quadratics split into a bilinear part and separable squares (p. 7); in the BARON tests, cuts at the root only (p. 16).
proof_devices: Rikun's sufficient condition (Lemma 2.2) and an explicit facet formula on a naive simplex (Proposition 2.3) (pp. 4-5)
facets correspond to basic feasible solutions of the vertex LP via affine independence (Theorem 2.4, pp. 5-6)
convergence of the convex envelope of an l.s.c. function as the box shrinks, for branch-and-bound convergence (Theorem 3.1, pp. 7-8)
three-term example where the multiterm envelope strictly dominates the termwise one (p. 8)
separability by connected components of the bilinear interaction graph, found by breadth-first search (pp. 12-13)
reduced cost of a vertex column equals the UBQP objective (Theorem 4.1, p. 13)
experiments: 135 random QCQPs (n 10-50, m 1 to 2n, densities 1, 0.5, 0.25), yardstick the best of BARON, MINOS, CONOPT, SNOPT at 100 s (p. 15); root: 76-104 s multiterm against 0.1-0.5 s termwise, 45-88% of the termwise gap closed (Table 1, p. 15); inside BARON with root cuts as relaxation-only constraints (1000 s): more solved, less time, smaller final gaps on non-trivial instances (Table 2, pp. 16-18).
positioning: Sorts QCQP relaxations into envelopes, RLT, Lagrangian and SDP/SOCP; builds on Rikun, Sherali, Tawarmalani and Sahinidis, Meyer and Floudas, Tardella; targets the termwise practice of BARON and LINDO (pp. 2-3).
writing: Theory first (envelope facets as LP bases), then the relaxation, then separation algorithms with a worked numeric example (bounds -3800, -3589, -3400 against the optimum -3300, p. 11), then tests, then a conclusion that names the cost (p. 18).
limits_future: Significantly more CPU time to construct (p. 18); separation LP exponential in a function's variables, so MUL suits many small bilinear functions (p. 12); reported gaps may be overstated since some instances were not solved globally (p. 16); future work: more general problems and cuts at every node (p. 18).

method_links.note: The stronger relaxation is kept polyhedral on purpose; its construction time is reported beside the gap it closes; stopping rules trade tightness against time; it is admitted only after BARON solves more instances faster with it (Method 5 step 3: multiterm LP inequalities as the cheaper object).

Tested inside the production solver with and without the cuts, but the cuts are generated outside and injected at the root through BARON's relaxation-only construct, not as a built-in module with a switch.
Yardstick is the best solution of four solvers at 100 s, not a certified optimum, on random instances rather than a public library; the authors say reported gaps may be overstated.
Trivial instances defined by an explicit size-and-density rule and set apart before effects are reported.

transferable: To separate a point from the convex envelope of a multilinear function over a box, solve the LP over the vertex constraints with objective a^T x* + b; an optimal basic solution is the most violated facet (Theorem 2.4, pp. 5-6; p. 10).

Price the vertex columns of that LP's dual with an unconstrained binary QP: run a multistart tabu heuristic first and go exact only when it finds no negative reduced cost (Theorem 4.1, Algorithm COL, pp. 13-14).
Split a bilinear function by the connected components of its interaction graph before separating, keeping separation problems small with no loss when the function is separable (pp. 12-13).
Prototype a relaxation outside a closed solver, pass its cuts as relaxation-only constraints, and compare solved counts, time and final gap with and without them (pp. 16-18).
Stop a cut loop on an iteration or time cap, or when the relative bound improvement stays below delta for K_seq consecutive rounds (p. 12).
coauthors: Xiaowei Bao (first author), Mohit Tawarmalani; Sahinidis corresponding (p. 1)

quotes.text: Our main goal is to maintain the polyhedrality enjoyed by termwise relaxations, while considerably improving the quality of the relaxation used.
Compared with the standard termwise relaxation of bilinear functions, the proposed relaxation requires significantly more CPU time to construct.
